strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: conditional generation of automotive radar point clouds from multi-view camera input, including RCS and Doppler attributes. This is relevant for multimodal simulation and data augmentation in autonomous driving.

The proposed representation is practical and well motivated: converting sparse radar point clouds into BEV density, RCS, and Doppler maps makes it possible to reuse efficient latent image diffusion machinery, while the deconvolution recovery step is a reasonable way to return to sparse points.

The method integrates geometry, semantics, and motion cues from pretrained foundation models in a spatially aligned BEV conditioning format. The ablations indicate that these cues contribute differently and meaningfully, especially semantic conditioning for RCS/statistical fidelity and velocity/appearance for Doppler behavior.

The evaluation goes beyond a single metric and includes geometric fidelity, attribute fidelity, distributional similarity, foreground-object statistics, qualitative results, multiple random seeds, recovery-method ablations, and a downstream detector sanity check.
The paper is generally clear, with helpful diagrams and implementation details, including training compute, inference time, recovery hyperparameters, and metric definitions in the supplement.
weaknesses: The experimental case for generality is limited. Results are shown on a single dataset, with night scenes filtered from training/evaluation and no cross-dataset or cross-radar-configuration validation, despite claims about scalable multimodal simulation.

The baseline comparison is not fully convincing. The main baseline is an adapted RGB2Point model, which is object/point-cloud oriented rather than a strong radar-generation baseline, and it uses only time t while RadarGen uses both t and t+delta t. This makes the reported gains harder to attribute solely to the proposed generative formulation.

Absolute performance remains modest: IoU@1m is 0.31, DA F1 is 0.24, and the downstream detector drops from 0.48 NDS on real radar to 0.30 on generated radar. These results are promising but still show a substantial realism gap relative to real radar.

The scene-editing and augmentation claims are mostly qualitative. The paper shows appealing examples, but does not quantify whether edited/generated radar improves detector training, robustness, or simulation utility in a controlled downstream experiment.

Several design choices are pragmatic but reduce physical grounding: elevation is discarded, RCS/Doppler maps are filled via nearest-neighbor Voronoi regions, and the model relies heavily on camera-derived foundation-model outputs. Failure modes under occlusion, poor depth/flow, reflective objects, weather, and low light are acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.

Reproducibility would benefit from more discussion of code/model release, preprocessing exactness, and dataset splits. The pipeline depends on multiple large pretrained components and a custom radar map/recovery process, so small implementation differences may materially affect results.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: generating automotive radar point clouds, including RCS and Doppler, from multi-view camera input. Radar simulation is important for autonomous-driving data generation, and the focus on processed radar point clouds is practically motivated.

The proposed representation is reasonable: converting sparse radar detections into BEV density, RCS, and Doppler maps makes the task compatible with latent image diffusion backbones, and the deconvolution-based recovery step is a sensible engineering choice.

The manuscript is generally clear and includes useful implementation details, metric definitions, and ablations. The evaluation attempts to cover geometry, attributes, distributional similarity, foreground objects, downstream detection, and qualitative scene editing.

RadarGen improves over the chosen RGB2Point baseline on many reported metrics, especially foreground hit rate and several MMD measures, suggesting the approach captures some radar statistics better than a direct feed-forward point generator.
weaknesses: The experimental case for acceptance is weak because the comparison set is very limited. The main baseline is an adapted object-centric RGB-to-point-cloud method that is not designed for sparse automotive radar scenes, uses only time t while RadarGen uses t and t+delta, and appears poorly matched to the task. The paper does not compare against closer radar point-cloud generation/simulation methods, deterministic camera/radar predictors, retrieval baselines, or stronger conditional generative baselines.

The reported gains are not uniformly convincing. Entire-area CD Full is worse than the baseline, many ablation differences are tiny relative to the standard deviations, and the BEV conditioning ablation is over-interpreted: removing appearance, semantics, or velocity often barely changes the core geometry and DA metrics. The direct multi-view conditioning model is competitive or better on several attribute-distribution metrics, weakening the claim that the proposed conditioning design is clearly superior beyond efficiency.

The evaluation is narrow: only one dataset and one radar setup are used, low-light scenes are filtered out, and generalization across datasets, sensors, weather, traffic density, or radar configurations is not tested. This is a major issue because the paper motivates RadarGen as scalable simulation compatible with broad visual datasets and simulators.

The paper claims probabilistic and stochastic radar generation, but diversity is evaluated only qualitatively with different seeds. There is no quantitative diversity/coverage analysis, calibration of generated distributions, or assessment of whether sampling captures multimodal radar uncertainty rather than merely adding noise around common patterns.

The downstream detection evidence is concerning. A detector trained on real radar drops from 0.48 NDS on real data to 0.30 on RadarGen data, and the authors explicitly state that the subtle differences are beyond scope. Since usefulness for perception and simulation is a central motivation, this gap needs deeper analysis, training-on-synthetic experiments, or sim-to-real augmentation results.

The scene-editing claim is supported only by a few qualitative examples. There is no systematic test of object insertion/removal/replacement, occlusion handling, temporal consistency, or failure cases, so the controllability claim remains anecdotal.

Several modeling choices are pragmatic but not physically well justified: dropping elevation, using Voronoi-filled RCS/Doppler maps, replicating scalar maps into RGB channels for a natural-image autoencoder, and retrieving attributes at deconvolved locations may introduce artifacts. The paper does not sufficiently analyze how these choices affect radar realism or physical validity.

Reproducibility and benchmark value are limited by the absence of standard evaluation protocols and unclear release commitments. The proposed metrics are useful, but many depend on threshold choices and foreground filtering; statistical significance and sensitivity to these choices are not analyzed.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored problem: generating automotive radar point clouds, including RCS and Doppler, from multi-view camera input. This is a meaningful contribution for multimodal simulation, where radar has lagged behind RGB and LiDAR generation.

The method is technically sensible and well motivated. Representing sparse radar as BEV density, RCS, and Doppler maps makes the problem compatible with efficient latent diffusion, while the explicit deconvolution recovery step is a principled way to return to sparse point clouds.

The conditioning design is strong: depth, semantic, and optical-flow cues from pretrained models are projected into BEV, giving the generator aligned geometric, semantic, and motion information rather than forcing it to infer everything directly from images.

The experimental package is fairly comprehensive for a new task. The authors report geometric fidelity, radar attribute fidelity, distributional metrics, foreground-object metrics, ablations over conditioning inputs, comparison to direct multi-view conditioning, reconstruction-method analysis, qualitative results, and a downstream detector evaluation.

Results are promising. RadarGen substantially improves over the adapted RGB2Point baseline on most metrics, especially foreground hit rate, density similarity, DA metrics, and MMD for RCS/Doppler. The fact that a detector trained on real radar obtains nontrivial NDS on generated radar further supports practical relevance.

The paper is clear and well organized, with useful supplementary details about metrics, training, inference, baseline implementation, and limitations. The scene-editing examples are a compelling demonstration of controllability.
weaknesses: The empirical comparison is still somewhat narrow. The main baseline is an adapted object/point-cloud model that appears poorly matched to radar scene generation and even fails to converge under the normalized objective. Stronger comparisons to recent radar point-cloud generation/simulation methods, even if adapted imperfectly, would make the case more convincing.

Evaluation is limited to one dataset and one radar configuration, after filtering out low-light night scenes. Since radar is especially valuable under adverse visual conditions, excluding such scenarios weakens the evidence for broader autonomous-driving utility.

The downstream detector result is encouraging but still shows a substantial gap to real radar: NDS drops from 0.48 on GT to 0.30 on RadarGen, with mAP 0.11 versus 0.38 and much worse velocity error. The paper notes this but does not deeply analyze what radar statistics remain missing.

Some claimed benefits rely heavily on upstream foundation models for depth, segmentation, and flow. This makes the system modular, but also transfers their failure modes into radar generation; the paper only provides qualitative limitation analysis rather than systematic stress tests for occlusion, night, weather, reflective surfaces, or camera degradation.

The ablation results are mixed in places. Removing individual BEV conditions often changes metrics only slightly, and direct multi-view conditioning is competitive or better on some attribute-distribution metrics, although more expensive. This somewhat tempers claims about the necessity of each conditioning component.

The representation discards elevation and uses Voronoi-filled dense attribute maps, which is pragmatic but may introduce artificial spatial correlations for RCS/Doppler and limit fidelity for modern higher-resolution radar. The impact of these modeling choices is not fully quantified beyond reconstruction metrics.

Reproducibility would benefit from clearer information about code/model release, preprocessing scripts, exact train/eval splits, and whether the proposed metrics and generated samples will be made available as a benchmark.
